analysis.one_liner: Phases fuel economy rules for SUVs, pickups, and federal fleet vehicles up to car-level standards.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have lifted mileage rules for SUVs and pickups to the level cars already met, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on January 30, 2003 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required light trucks — the category covering SUVs, pickups, and minivans — to average at least 27.5 miles per gallon by the 2011 model year, the same standard cars already had to meet, after stepping up through 23.5, 24.8, and 26.1 mpg in earlier model years [S3]. It would also have extended fuel economy rules to the heaviest SUVs weighing up to 10,000 pounds, which were exempt from mileage standards at the time, and required federal agencies to buy vehicles averaging 3 mpg more efficient by 2007 and 6 mpg more efficient by 2010 [S3]. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, especially households that buy SUVs, pickups, and minivans, would save on gasoline over the life of their vehicles as the trucks they shop for become more efficient. Federal taxpayers would benefit both from lower government fuel bills and, indirectly, from reduced national oil consumption. Autoworkers and dealers gain nothing directly, though retooling for efficient trucks would have required manufacturing investment.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the average fuel economy standard for light trucks — SUVs, pickups, and minivans — from its then-current level to 27.5 mpg for the 2011 model year, the same standard that applied to cars, after interim steps of 23.5 mpg (2008 models), 24.8 mpg (2009), and 26.1 mpg (2010).

Extends federal fuel economy standards to vehicles rated up to 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight starting in 2011 — a category that includes the largest SUVs, which at the time were not treated as passenger cars and faced no comparable mileage requirement.

Requires each executive agency to buy new vehicles averaging at least 3 mpg better than its fiscal 2005 baseline by September 30, 2007, and 6 mpg better by September 30, 2010, cutting the government's own fuel use.

By lifting the mileage of the fastest-growing vehicle segment, the bill would have reduced household gasoline spending and national oil consumption without raising taxes or mandating any particular technology — it set an outcome and let manufacturers choose how to meet it.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers whose profits depended on large SUVs and pickups — mainly the domestic manufacturers — would bear the cost of engineering and retooling to meet the higher standards, and would likely pass some of it on in vehicle prices. Federal agencies would face somewhat higher upfront vehicle-procurement costs for the fleet requirement. Drivers of big trucks would face higher sticker prices in exchange for lower fuel bills.

drawbacks.text: The bill left all light trucks built before model year 2008 untouched, so no current truck or SUV benefited and the changeover would have been spread over four model years starting in 2008 — a slow phase-in that softened both the savings and the disruption.

The standard was a flat fleet-average mpg number rather than one adjusted for vehicle size, the design automakers had long argued forced trade-offs between fuel economy, vehicle utility, and safety, since meeting a single average can pressure makers to build lighter vehicles.

The federal fleet mandate imposed real procurement costs on executive agencies — they would have had to buy more expensive, more efficient vehicles on a fixed schedule — a cost ultimately carried by taxpayers even if repaid through lower fuel spending over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were concrete and well-targeted: extending the existing car standard of 27.5 mpg to the truck category would have closed the loophole that let manufacturers sell gas-hungry SUVs under laxer rules, with real savings for drivers and less oil use. The costs fell on a concentrated industry that had profited from that loophole, and the bill's phase-in was gradual enough to be manageable — this was a moderate version of CAFE reform, not an aggressive one. The honest objections are the flat-average design, which critics said could shift the vehicle mix in ways automakers opposed, and the unaddressed question of who absorbs compliance costs between manufacturers and buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on January 30, 2003 with an initial group of cosponsors that included Republicans Olympia Snowe and Susan Collins alongside a dozen Democrats and Independent Jim Jeffords.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the committee with jurisdiction over fuel economy standards.
The action history shows no further steps of any kind: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 108th Congress, which ended January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that sold large SUVs and pickups — the manufacturers the bill would have forced to build more efficient trucks — were better off, since no new mileage requirements ever advanced. Drivers who bought trucks in those years paid for more gasoline than the bill would have saved them.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, along with the chamber's lone Independent and 3 of 51 Senate Republicans, for 18 cosponsors in total.

against.name: John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill; the record shows referral was the only action ever taken.

against.name: Major U.S. automakers
against.what_they_did: Publicly fought mandated increases in fuel economy standards during this period, arguing higher mileage requirements would impose heavy compliance costs and limit the large vehicles their profits depended on.

against.name: United Auto Workers
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory fuel economy increases during this period, arguing they would raise vehicle costs and threaten autoworker jobs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 18 cosponsors spanned parties — 14 of 48 Senate Democrats, 3 of 51 Senate Republicans, and the chamber's lone Independent — but no vote was ever held, so opposition never appeared on any recorded roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have forced truck fleets to average 27.5 mpg by 2011, the standard cars already met, and extended rules to the largest SUVs for the first time. Manufacturers had built their profits around the loophole that let big trucks avoid car-level mileage rules, so compliance meant redesigning their best-selling, highest-margin vehicles.

Higher mileage standards reduce gasoline demand over time, trimming sales in the country's largest fuel market. The industry's interest in this bill ran against drivers, who save money when vehicles burn less fuel.
